goal: Teach Year-2 physics students to turn a familiar calculation into an ordered algorithm, trace and complete a MATLAB loop, make one controlled change, diagnose defects from evidence, validate a result, and transfer the same reasoning to a supplied radioactive-decay process.

style.color_palette: open warm-white canvas; deep navy #243B53 for titles and structure; dusty blue #6E8FB3 for model and process content; quiet sage #7AA69B for expected or validated states; muted ochre #C7A35A for occasional prompts; subdued coral #BF7A70 only for genuine defects or physical failure

deck_context.source_summary: Week 02 keeps the familiar one-dimensional vertical-launch model so the new cognitive load is algorithmic rather than mathematical. The lecture moves from prediction to one calculation, then to a repeatable recipe, paired index tracing, a MATLAB loop, a genuine storage-line completion, a controlled parameter change, exact sampled evidence, a supplied radioactive-decay transfer, defect diagnosis, layered validation, and an exit ticket.
deck_context.core_claim: A loop becomes trustworthy when every pass has a clear input, current value, update, matching output slot, stopping point, check, and physical interpretation.
deck_context.locked_vertical_model: y(t) = y0 + v0 t - (1/2) g t^2; upward is positive; air resistance is neglected; gravity is constant; y0_m = 0 m; v0_mps = 20 m s^-1; g_mps2 = 9.81 m s^-2; t_s = 0:0.5:4 s.
deck_context.controlled_comparison: Use the same t_s = 0:0.5:4 s grid. For v0 = 20 m s^-1, the highest sampled point is 20.38 m at 2.0 s and y(4 s) = 1.52 m. For v0 = 15 m s^-1, the highest sampled point is 11.46375 m at 1.5 s and y(4 s) = -18.48 m. The no-impact model continues to 4 s; y = 0 is the launch reference, not an automatic stopping rule.
deck_context.decay_transfer: N(t) = N0 exp(-lambda t), lambda = log(2)/half_life_h, N0_counts = 800, half_life_h = 6.0, t_decay_h = 0:1:24, N(0 h) = 800, N(6 h) = 400, and N(24 h) = 50.
deck_context.exactness: Equations, code, indices, numerical values, units, signs, assertions, blanks, and plot data are strict teaching content. Do not invent, paraphrase, or approximate them.
deck_context.scope_guard: Do not introduce a differential equation, half-life derivation, stochastic model, fitting, Newton cooling, eigenproblem, advanced root-finding stress case, try/catch, or advanced debugging mechanism into the Week 02 Core lecture.

slides.title: Numerical Algorithms: Turn physical reasoning into pseudocode, loops, and fixes
slides.intent: Open with the driving question and show a loop as an extension of a physical calculation.
key_points: A familiar equation can be evaluated one time at a time.
An algorithm makes the order visible.
A loop makes repetition explicit.
Evidence still needs checking and physical interpretation.
slides.local_context: Continue the familiar vertical-motion story while shifting the focus to ordered repetition, debugging, and validation.

slides.title: Predict the motion before asking MATLAB to repeat anything
slides.intent: Reactivate the physical prediction before introducing loop syntax.
key_points: Choose upward as positive.
The ball starts at y = 0 m.
It rises to one maximum, then falls.
The prediction is our first debugging reference.
slides.local_context: Use the locked vertical model with y0 = 0 m, v0 = 20 m s^-1, and g = 9.81 m s^-2. Do not show MATLAB code yet.

slides.title: Fix the model, then ask what changes
slides.intent: Separate fixed physical inputs from the single scalar that changes on each loop pass.
key_points: Use y(t) = y0 + v0 t - (1/2) g t^2.
Keep y0 = 0 m, v0 = 20 m s^-1, and g = 9.81 m s^-2 fixed.
Choose ordered times t_s = 0:0.5:4 s.
One evaluation gives one position.
slides.local_context: Explain that current_time_s changes while the model stays fixed. Keep all equation symbols, signs, values, and units exact.

slides.title: One calculation is four small jobs
slides.intent: Give students a plain-language algorithm before MATLAB syntax.
key_points: Input stores parameters and ordered times.
Calculate evaluates the model at the current time.
Store writes one result to the matching slot.
Check compares the result with something already known.
slides.local_context: Use the four-job sequence INPUT -> CALCULATE -> STORE -> CHECK. Make the output slot distinct from the current value.

layout.composition: four connected stations with a lower one-pass teaching band showing one pass = one time -> one position

visual_elements.main_visual: four labelled stations and directional arrows

constraints: Use sage only for the CHECK state.
Do not repeat the same oversized prompt box used elsewhere.

slides.title: An index traces both selection and storage
slides.intent: Combine index mapping and the first two loop passes so an abstract address is tied to a physical moment and an output slot.
key_points: MATLAB indexing starts at 1.
t_s(sample_index) selects the current physical time.
y_m(sample_index) selects the matching output slot.
Pass 1: index 1, t = 0 s, y = 0 m; pass 2: index 2, t = 0.5 s, y = 8.77375 m.
slides.local_context: Show two trace cards with the exact fields index, current time, calculation, and stored result. The same sample_index must highlight both the input and output row.

slides.title: Calculate one value; store it in the matching slot
slides.intent: Show scalar selection and calculation while delaying the storage action for the next bounded task.
key_points: Preallocate one output slot per time.
Loop from 1 to n_samples.
Read current_time_s = t_s(sample_index).
Calculate current_position_m from the scalar time; then ask where it belongs.
slides.local_context: Use a readable, complete code fragment except for the storage statement. Keep current_time_s and current_position_m as scalar MATLAB identifiers. Do not reveal the missing storage expression.

slides.title: Your turn: complete the storage line
slides.intent: Require one controlled implementation action and its physical meaning.
key_points: The blank must store the current scalar result.
It must use the current index.
It must not overwrite one fixed element.
The first stored value should remain 0 m.
slides.local_context: Render one genuine blank in the code scaffold: y_m(sample_index) = ______; Do not include the answer expression anywhere on the slide. Keep the sentence frame current value -> matching slot.

slides.title: A second process can use the same loop logic
slides.intent: Introduce radioactive decay as a safe structural analogue without adding new numerical-method theory.
key_points: Start with N0_counts = 800 and half_life_h = 6.0.
Use hourly times t_decay_h = 0:1:24.
Expect a decreasing count.
Half-life checks predict N(6 h) = 400 and N(24 h) = 50.
slides.local_context: Use the exact supplied model N(t) = N0 exp(-lambda t), lambda = log(2)/half_life_h. Do not derive the half-life relation, introduce a differential equation, or discuss stochastic counting.

slides.title: Transfer challenge — write the loop in plain language first
slides.intent: Move the loop pattern to radioactive decay while keeping the implementation demand bounded and unsolved.
key_points: Input the count, half-life, decay constant, and hourly times.
For each index, select the current time.
Calculate one count and store it in the matching output slot.
Check the half-life point and stop after the final hour.
slides.local_context: Render unsolved pseudocode only. Include a blank at the storage action and the prompt What should be true at 6 h? Do not show MATLAB code or the completed answer.

slides.title: Diagnose the defect before editing the code
slides.intent: Give students a concrete decision path across syntax, array/operator, and physical/logical defects.
key_points: Syntax defects stop MATLAB reading the intended structure.
Indexing or operator defects can run while selecting or storing the wrong thing.
Physical or logical defects can produce plausible numbers with wrong physics.
The code ran is not a correctness test.
slides.local_context: Use short exact examples: missing end; fixed output index y_m(1) or t_s^2 instead of t_s.^2; wrong gravity sign or wrong units. Pair each with symptom and evidence.

slides.title: Use evidence to locate the first bad pass
slides.intent: Turn the defect categories into a repeatable evidence-based repair habit.
key_points: Record the symptom.
Locate the line and first bad pass.
Compare code with pseudocode or the physical model.
Change one item, rerun, and validate numerically and physically.
slides.local_context: Show six workflow stages: symptom -> first bad pass -> model/pseudocode -> one change -> rerun -> two checks. Examples may include missing end, 1:(n_samples+1), t_s^2 vs t_s.^2, y_m(1) overwrite, wrong gravity sign, and wrong units.

slides.title: A passing check can still miss wrong physics
slides.intent: Show what one check proves, what it misses, and why physical interpretation remains part of correctness.
key_points: y(0) = 0 m is a known initial-value check.
assert(y_m(1) == y0_m) checks the first stored value.
A wrong gravity sign can still pass at t = 0.
Compare direction and shape with the physical prediction: check the number and the meaning.
slides.local_context: Use a validation stack: model check, code/output check, and physical-meaning check. The wrong-sign trajectory should be visually plausible as a curve but physically inconsistent.

slides.title: Exit ticket — explain the loop to a future you
slides.intent: Consolidate the Core reasoning chain without revealing answers and preview the two-equation circuit context in Week 03.
key_points: Put input, calculation, output, and check in order.
Explain what t_s(sample_index) selects.
Identify one defect and its evidence.
State one validation and one physical conclusion.
slides.local_context: End with four response cards: Order, Trace, Diagnose, Validate. Add a small bridge from the loop recipe to Week 03's 2 x 2 circuit model. Do not include the answers.
